subsystems.name: Oracle
subsystems.role: marks the solution state by flipping its sign, so the search knows what to look for.

subsystems.name: Diffusion operator
subsystems.role: reflects all amplitudes about their average, which amplifies the marked state's probability.
parts: phase flip about the zero state

subsystems.name: Quantum register
subsystems.role: holds the equal superposition of all N candidates.

subsystems.name: Control and readout
subsystems.role: runs the Grover iterations and measures the final state.

subsystems.name: Error mitigation and correction
subsystems.role: keeps the quantum state coherent long enough for many iterations.

buildSteps.title: Encode the search problem
buildSteps.detail: Express the problem as a Boolean function that returns true for the target state(s); this defines the search space size N.

buildSteps.title: Design the oracle circuit
buildSteps.detail: Build a reversible quantum circuit that applies a phase flip to the target state(s) and leaves all others unchanged. This is often the hardest part.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the uniform superposition
buildSteps.detail: Apply a Hadamard gate to every qubit in the register, creating an equal superposition of all 2^n states.

buildSteps.title: Apply Grover iterations
buildSteps.detail: Repeat the oracle followed by the diffusion operator about √N times. Each iteration rotates the state vector slightly toward the target.

buildSteps.title: Measure the register
buildSteps.detail: Read out the qubits; the target state appears with high probability.

buildSteps.title: Verify and repeat
buildSteps.detail: Classically check the output; if incorrect, run again or adjust the number of iterations.

buildSteps.title: Integrate into a larger application
buildSteps.detail: For constraint solving or cryptanalysis, embed the oracle in a classical-quantum loop that maps the problem and uses the result.

prerequisites.why: current devices have tens to hundreds of noisy qubits; useful Grover tasks need many more and better fidelity.
small logical qubits have been demonstrated, but a fault-tolerant machine with thousands of logical qubits does not exist.
turning real-world problems into compact quantum circuits is an active research area and often dominates the cost.
microwave and laser control of qubits works, but scaling to thousands of qubits with low crosstalk is hard.
classical computers define the problem, verify results and orchestrate repeated runs.

pathway.milestone: demonstrations on a handful of qubits for toy search problems
pathway.unlocks: proof that amplitude amplification works on real hardware.

pathway.milestone: early fault-tolerant processors with tens of logical qubits
pathway.unlocks: quantum advantage for small constraint-satisfaction or database-search problems.

pathway.milestone: fault-tolerant machines with hundreds to thousands of logical qubits
pathway.unlocks: practical speedups for optimization and some symmetric-key attacks.
cryptanalysis of widely used symmetric ciphers (e.g. AES-128 reduced from 2^128 to 2^64 operations) and large-scale search.
